Knysna Elephant -- the last lonely elephant

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Just how many Knysna elephants are there left?

Unique Selling Point:
This week SANparks confirmed something they have suspected for the last 20 years -there is only one Knysna elephant and is now the last free-roaming and most isolated elephant in the world. She is the last survivor from herds that once roamed the forests, the rest have been hunted out. Elephants are social creatures, especially female elephants, they move in family groups, but this poor female has spent the last 20 lonely years hiding in the deep impenetrable indigenous forests above Knysna and Sedgefield. The elusive Knysna elephants have become figures of folk law, forests creatures that appear and disappear. For years the numbers have been debated, and can they save themselves? Are there both male and females and with protection like the Addo elephant will their numbers recover? In 1920 when they establish Addo Elephant Park there were 16 elephants now there are 480. This week SANParks confirmed, that their camera traps, set up along ancient elephant paths, recording her movements for the last 15 months, only capture one female. The forest is so dense there are only certain routes and they have mapped them extensively, and not once over 4 years has another elephant ever been captured. It comes on the back of the Landmark Foundations study, done two years done prior to this study, which also recorded only one female. These elephants evolved within this forest terrain and this is our last opportunity to re-establish a population with the resident genetics. But why keep searching for the elephants? So much time and money have been spent to the existence of the elephant because they are the most southern free ranging elephants and have a specific genetic adaptation to existing in the forest despite being Savannah elephants and they play a critical role is this lush eco-system. Time is running out and Patterson "find" of 5 elephants and possibly one male has only set back the efforts to intervene. Extensive consultation is taking place with all the stake holders around the forest about how they can reintroduce more elephants. The Addo to Eden corridor is a conservation project that hopes to open the passage but that is a long way off. Conservationist are asking how much more evidence do we need before we do something to rescue the last remaining forest elephant from a extinction? What now that they have confirmed their suspicion? What urgent action? What is the update in the stakeholder involvement? The camera traps has also documented other threatened species like the coastal leopard, ratels, blue duiker giving conservationists far more information about the habitat than they had before and now they have footage to prove it.

Summary:
SANParks, who are the controlling authority of not just the forests, but also the Garden Route lakes system, says that their camera traps and evidence collected by rangers indicates that only one cow still survives, a 45-year-old matriarch who is reaching the end of her reproductive years.
But naturalist and conservationist, Gareth Patterson, disputes this, saying his research indicates there are five or six surviving elephants. Patterson’s work in the Knysna forests has been documented in “The Search for the Knysna Elephants”, a documentary screened internationally by Animal Planet. His elephant research is ongoing, alongside research into another mysterious denizen of the southern Cape, the relatively unknown coastal leopards.Unfortunately Patterson claims set back attempts to remedy the lonely elephants situation, his study created the impression there was a family of both male and females that could survive for hundreds of years.

Further information:
There were once up to a thousand elephants roaming over 121 000 hectares of the Outeniqua and Tsitsikamma Forests, the then southernmost population left in Africa after their extinction in the Western Cape – the last elephant in the Cape Peninsula was shot in 1704, and the herds in the Overberg area west of Knysna were killed off by 1800. By 1870, only an estimated 400 elephants remained in the area from Knysna to Addo.
In 1919, professional hunter Major Philip Jacobus Pretorius was hired by the Cape government to exterminate the last of the elephants. The Administrator of the Cape, Sir Frederic de Waal (De Waal Drive) wanted them completely exterminated. But it was finally decided to leave a small herd of 16 in the Addo Reserve. In just over a year, Pretorius shot 115 elephants.
Ever since then, sightings have been elusive, with there generally being believed to be between four and 14 elephants surviving at any one time. A 1970 survey estimated 14 elephants; a 1996 study found that the elephants were functionally extinct, with just one adult female left. In 1986, Daleen Matthee’s book “Circles In A Forest” (Kringe in die Bos) was published, became a best-seller, and was made into a Hollywood movie, and gave new impetus to the plight and conservation of the Knysna elephants.
In September 2000, forest guard Wilfred Oraai videotaped a young bull from a distance of about 30 metres. Patterson has collected numerous fresh samples of elephant dung for DNA analysis by geneticist Lori Eggert from the University of Missouri in Columbia, and on this he bases his estimate of at least five females, and at one stage, three bulls and two calves.
Despite the DNA evidence, officials insisted only one elephant survived, an elusive female known as 'The Matriarch' or 'Oupoot', making the Knysna elephant functionally extinct. In 1994, three cows were brought from the Kruger National Park and released into a boma at Diepwalle, and then released into the forest. One cow soon died, they were brought to Knysna in the winter. THe other two were very young about 3 years old and they could not keep up with the matriarch who roams about 30 kms everyday. Eventually the remaining two preferred raiding farm pastures to the forests, and they were removed to Shamwari private reserve five years later.

Since then, there have been competing claims, the latest being those of Patterson and SANParks this past week: in 2002, sightings suggested there were three elephants; in 2007, faecal DNA analysis pointed at five remaining females, but this was not confirmed by sightings and other evidence; in 2015, 18 months of grid camera trapping of the forests by the Landmark Foundation (Dr Bool Smuts) indicated only one matriarch remained.

Pattersons claims have been disputed by scientists saying DNA sampling of elephant dung is far more complex but everyone agrees that SOMETHING has to be done urgently. Since 1994 conservationists have learnt a lot more about elephant relocation and elephants from Addo would be better suited than from Kruger.

Press Release:


The Last Knysna Elephant
Thousands of elephants once roamed the dense forests of Knysna but over the last 100 years they have been hunted to virtual extinction. For decades, debates have raged on about whether the last-sighted elephant in the forest is one of a family or a single, lone female. Now camera traps, set up along ancient elephant paths, record this heart-breaking story. Carte Blanche joins the tracking team on this remarkable search.
Producer: Liz Fish
Presenter: Derek Watts
Watch the trailer


Script:


Script: Somewhere, deep and hidden, southern Africa’s last forest elephants tread a lonely path through their last fortress. Once more than a thousand of these giants ghosted through the Tsitsikamma and Outeniqua Forests, Africa’s southernmost surviving elephants.
Their systematic eradication – for sport and ivory – and their uncomfortable coexistence with woodcutters and farmers was the subject of acclaimed novelist Dalene Matthee’s CIRCLES IN THE FOREST. Translated for a global audience, the book also became a prominent school set work.
Links “The most tragic incident in the saga of this elephant population goes back exactly a hundred years ago that is when the administrator of the Cape Sir Fredrick De Wall wanted them completely exterminated and hired a professional hunter who in the space of just over a year shot 115 elephants
Script: They retreated deep into the forest and became masters of disguise, changing their diet to suit their new home.
Script: We’re heading into the mountains over rough mountain tracks in search of the mysterious elephants with SANParks scientist Lizette Moolman. She’s spent the last 5 years trying to establish just how many elephants actually roam these forests. They’re so elusive; she set up 80 camera traps at 40 stations
Derek: When you did the survey how extensive was the coverage of the camera traps.
Lizette: Think of it the whole entire elephant range …and what we did is we made sure that the whole entire area is covered with cameras stations and that the areas between those cameras stations are not so big that elephants can hide in that area
Link: The debate of what to do about the Knysna elephants and how many actually roam these dense forests has been raging for the last 50 years
Script: The two men who know them intimately are trackers Wilfred Orai and Karel Mswati. They’ve been on the trail for 31 years.
Upsound
Script: They’ve guided countless researchers through this dense terrain
Karel: She is like a person she understands us we have walked with her through the bush and if she gets stressed by us we stay away from her for a bit she reasonable
Derek “What sounds does she make
Upsound: Karel elephant trumpet and Derek laughing
Script: Photographer and forester Hylton Herd began working on the elephant tracking project in 1994
Hylton: When one looks at those photographs it's amazing how they differ in terms of how the animal comes across one day particularly when this photograph was from above it kind of like just gave it a bull of look about it And then one day you …can see the mammary glands and it looks clear that it's it's it's a cow.
Script: Slowly, through looking at the distinctive ear markings, Hylton realised they were looking at the same female. In 1994, Conservationist were concerned about the shrinking population
Links: 3 baby elephants survivors of a cull were brought in from Kruger national park and kept in a boma right here to get used to the forest
Script: The hope was the matriah would teach the Kruger babies the secret paths of the forest, and what to eat. But it was winter, and the forest was cold and wet. One baby died of pneumonia
Hylton: they actually did meet up and actually walk together for about two months or so and then eventually there was a big skirmish
Script: The two Kruger elephants fled the forest and began wrecking havoc on the farms. The project was abandoned, and the Kruger babies were relocated to Shamwari nature reserve.
Link: There was a great flutter and renewed hope in 2007 when conservationist Gareth Patterson claimed he had found DNA evidence of 5 young cows. He believed there was a viable population along with some roaming bulls.
Script: Gareth had heard about American conservation geneticist, Lori Eggert, who extracted DNA from the dung’s mucus residue.
Gareth: I did two DNA studies in 2007 and 2009. And that was remarkable because we picked up the same five females in 2009 as we did in 2007 and we actually picked up sixth female, which we missed the first time round.
Derek: But didn't you feel there were some roaming bulls.
Gareth: Yes I felt at the time that field studies indicated that there was at least three bulls and we had calves and the fact that the had been births
Script: But these findings have been questioned as new scientific methods emerge.
Lizette: I used to work in a lab as a molecular biologist and there are so many things downstream from when you pick the dung up until when you get your fingerprint ….that technique especially on dung is not like a forensic DNA result.
Derek: using blood for example.
Lizette: Yes, But it's almost impossible to get that technique to give you a forensic definite answer. And I think that's what people often don't understand. However at the time it was good science and it was what was available
Derek “You cover a lot of ground Lizette
Lizette ”well the elephant range is about 185 sq kilometres and she also crosses two river gorges where we also have cameras
Script: When Lizette started her camera trap study in 2014, she really hoped she would find these elephants, but slowly she had to accept what she was seeing. In the 5000 images taken over 15 months, all she found was one lone female, aged about 45 years.
Derek: [16:45:50] And you're convinced just the one female.
Lizette: [16:45:52] Yes. Yeah.
Derek: [17:12:54. What do you think.
Karel: [17:13:21] Well the in last time I saw in the elephant directly was in 1990 I saw two elephants the younger elephant from the back and the old mother we think she died years ago in 1991
Script: She often removes things she doesn’t think belong in the forest. She breaks down gates, removes signs and overturns machines. And the closest thing she can find to a friend is this logger. She is a lonely solitary figure
Link: What a miserable fate when you consider that elephants are social creatures and she has been wandering these paths alone now for the last 20 years or more. We have allowed these elephants to go functionally extinct
Script: The camera traps also revealed the secret life of the forest, and it is thriving. Bush pig, bush buck, leopards at all their stations, Caracals, Cape clawless otters and southern Africa’s most endangered buck, the Blue Duiker. The bad news is that more and more people are invading their sanctuary with mountain bikes and off-road motorbikes, hemming them in.
Park Manager Paddy Gordon says this information is critical on how to manage the forest
Paddy: And what is also a very tragic conservation story is that we took so long to know what is going on Paddy: As conservationist is we need to constantly look forward. What are we going to do next and are we going to do it differently because we don't want to sit here 10 20 years later. Oh look we've got the last leopard but the last Rooikat.
Script: Gareth is a well-known conservation figure, and makes his living writing books on the elephants and guiding walks. He just doesn’t believe the results from the Sanparks cameras or the Landmark Foundation’s leopard study, which covered over 18 000 hectares. He thinks the elephant range is bigger:
Gareth: Scientific papers have shown within species you've got animals that are camera shy and camera curious and with this particular female she's incredibly curious not only visually but also by hearing so they can actually evade at the same time.
Derek: But Gareth she's got cameras in opposing directions which would actually film any animal turning around.
Gareth: Yeah I mean this one individual just loves the cameras she really does.
Derek: But the other five or more camera shy. Don’t you ever have doubts that this is a Houdini act of major proportions.
Gareth: And they will prove us wrong time and time again they will that how they are
Lizette: The recent technology uses black flash so since then the scientific community has really embraced this kind of technique
Derek: [18:17:23] Isnt your optimism about the number of elephants be coloured by your business of books and tours
Gareth: [18:17:32] No at all not at all no.
Garth: She is not alone. There are others out there but it’s an imperiled population and we need to intervene to bring in others here. How we go about that. I don't know.
Script: Sanparks is convinced there is only one and, and saving the last free-roaming, wild elephant is extremely complex because she wanders across plantations, farmlands and forests. She belongs to everyone, and no one
Paddy “ If I bring elephant in I transfer that legal accountability immediately towards myself so there is a big legal implication to bringing elephants in. Add to that a very fragmented forest system no fences to keep the elephant in. Uh very expensive farmland on the on the outskirts that could be damaged by elephant and go rogue
Derek: Exactly what are your plans?
Paddy: Remember she is not a unique species. She's the same species as the Addo elephant... She's not a forest species. What is unique is that she's learned behaviours that makes her survive in the Knysna forest. So she learned from her mother and our belief is that the only thing to do now is that she needs to pass that information on to another one and then build from there. Basically buying time
Script: And there is a very real danger she could die before an ethical solution to this complex conservation dilemma is found.

The project was abandoned, and the Kruger babies were relocated to Shamwari nature reserve. Link: There was a great flutter and renewed hope in 2007 when conservationist Gareth Patterson claimed he had found DNA evidence of 5 young cows. He believed there was a viable population along with some roaming bulls. Script: Gareth had heard about American conservation geneticist, Lori Eggert, who extracted DNA from the dung’s mucus residue. Gareth: I did two DNA studies in 2007 and 2009. And that was remarkable because we picked up the same five females in 2009 as we did in 2007 and we actually picked up sixth female, which we missed the first time round. Derek: But didn't you feel there were some roaming bulls. Gareth: Yes I felt at the time that field studies indicated that there was at least three bulls and we had calves and the fact that the had been births Script: But these findings have been questioned as new scientific methods emerge. Lizette: I used to work in a lab as a molecular biologist and there are so many things downstream from when you pick the dung up until when you get your fingerprint ….that technique especially on dung is not like a forensic DNA result. Derek: using blood for example. Lizette: Yes, But it's almost impossible to get that technique to give you a forensic definite answer. And I think that's what people often don't understand. However at the time it was good science and it was what was available Derek “You cover a lot of ground Lizette Lizette ”well the elephant range is about 185 sq kilometres and she also crosses two river gorges where we also have cameras Script: When Lizette started her camera trap study in 2014, she really hoped she would find these elephants, but slowly she had to accept what she was seeing. In the 5000 images taken over 15 months, all she found was one lone female, aged about 45 years. Derek: [16:45:50] And you're convinced just the one female. Lizette: [16:45:52] Yes. Yeah. Derek: [17:12:54. What do you think. Karel: [17:13:21] Well the in last time I saw in the elephant directly was in 1990 I saw two elephants the younger elephant from the back and the old mother we think she died years ago in 1991 Script: She often removes things she doesn’t think belong in the forest. She breaks down gates, removes signs and overturns machines. And the closest thing she can find to a friend is this logger. She is a lonely solitary figure Link: What a miserable fate when you consider that elephants are social creatures and she has been wandering these paths alone now for the last 20 years or more. We have allowed these elephants to go functionally extinct Script: The camera traps also revealed the secret life of the forest, and it is thriving. Bush pig, bush buck, leopards at all their stations, Caracals, Cape clawless otters and southern Africa’s most endangered buck, the Blue Duiker. The bad news is that more and more people are invading their sanctuary with mountain bikes and off-road motorbikes, hemming them in. Park Manager Paddy Gordon says this information is critical on how to manage the forest Paddy: And what is also a very tragic conservation story is that we took so long to know what is going on Paddy: As conservationist is we need to constantly look forward. What are we going to do next and are we going to do it differently because we don't want to sit here 10 20 years later. Oh look we've got the last leopard but the last Rooikat. Script: Gareth is a well-known conservation figure, and makes his living writing books on the elephants and guiding walks. He just doesn’t believe the results from the Sanparks cameras or the Landmark Foundation’s leopard study, which covered over 18 000 hectares. He thinks the elephant range is bigger: Gareth: Scientific papers have shown within species you've got animals that are camera shy and camera curious and with this particular female she's incredibly curious not only visually but also by hearing so they can actually evade at the same time. Derek: But Gareth she's got cameras in opposing directions which would actually film any animal turning around. Gareth: Yeah I mean this one individual just loves the cameras she really does. Derek: But the other five or more camera shy. Don’t you ever have doubts that this is a Houdini act of major proportions. Gareth: And they will prove us wrong time and time again they will that how they are Lizette: The recent technology uses black flash so since then the scientific community has really embraced this kind of technique Derek: [18:17:23] Isnt your optimism about the number of elephants be coloured by your business of books and tours Gareth: [18:17:32] No at all not at all no. Garth: She is not alone. There are others out there but it’s an imperiled population and we need to intervene to bring in others here. How we go about that. I don't know. Script: Sanparks is convinced there is only one and, and saving the last free-roaming, wild elephant is extremely complex because she wanders across plantations, farmlands and forests. She belongs to everyone, and no one Paddy “ If I bring elephant in I transfer that legal accountability immediately towards myself so there is a big legal implication to bringing elephants in. Add to that a very fragmented forest system no fences to keep the elephant in. Uh very expensive farmland on the on the outskirts that could be damaged by elephant and go rogue Derek: Exactly what are your plans? Paddy: Remember she is not a unique species. She's the same species as the Addo elephant... She's not a forest species. What is unique is that she's learned behaviours that makes her survive in the Knysna forest. So she learned from her mother and our belief is that the only thing to do now is that she needs to pass that information on to another one and then build from there. Basically buying time Script: And there is a very real danger she could die before an ethical solution to this complex conservation dilemma is found.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Just how many Knysna elephants are there left?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This week SANparks confirmed something they have suspected for the last 20 years -there is only one Knysna elephant and is now the last free-roaming and most isolated elephant in the world. She is the last survivor from herds that once roamed the forests, the rest have been hunted out. Elephants are social creatures, especially female elephants, they move in family groups, but this poor female has spent the last 20 lonely years hiding in the deep impenetrable indigenous forests above Knysna and Sedgefield. The elusive Knysna elephants have become figures of folk law, forests creatures that appear and disappear. For years the numbers have been debated, and can they save themselves? Are there both male and females and with protection like the Addo elephant will their numbers recover? In 1920 when they establish Addo Elephant Park there were 16 elephants now there are 480. This week SANParks confirmed, that their camera traps, set up along ancient elephant paths, recording her movements for the last 15 months, only capture one female. The forest is so dense there are only certain routes and they have mapped them extensively, and not once over 4 years has another elephant ever been captured. It comes on the back of the Landmark Foundations study, done two years done prior to this study, which also recorded only one female. These elephants evolved within this forest terrain and this is our last opportunity to re-establish a population with the resident genetics. But why keep searching for the elephants? So much time and money have been spent to the existence of the elephant because they are the most southern free ranging elephants and have a specific genetic adaptation to existing in the forest despite being Savannah elephants and they play a critical role is this lush eco-system. Time is running out and Patterson "find" of 5 elephants and possibly one male has only set back the efforts to intervene. Extensive consultation is taking place with all the stake holders around the forest about how they can reintroduce more elephants. The Addo to Eden corridor is a conservation project that hopes to open the passage but that is a long way off. Conservationist are asking how much more evidence do we need before we do something to rescue the last remaining forest elephant from a extinction? What now that they have confirmed their suspicion? What urgent action? What is the update in the stakeholder involvement? The camera traps has also documented other threatened species like the coastal leopard, ratels, blue duiker giving conservationists far more information about the habitat than they had before and now they have footage to prove it.
metadata.Summary: SANParks, who are the controlling authority of not just the forests, but also the Garden Route lakes system, says that their camera traps and evidence collected by rangers indicates that only one cow still survives, a 45-year-old matriarch who is reaching the end of her reproductive years. But naturalist and conservationist, Gareth Patterson, disputes this, saying his research indicates there are five or six surviving elephants. Patterson’s work in the Knysna forests has been documented in “The Search for the Knysna Elephants”, a documentary screened internationally by Animal Planet. His elephant research is ongoing, alongside research into another mysterious denizen of the southern Cape, the relatively unknown coastal leopards.Unfortunately Patterson claims set back attempts to remedy the lonely elephants situation, his study created the impression there was a family of both male and females that could survive for hundreds of years.
metadata.Further information: There were once up to a thousand elephants roaming over 121 000 hectares of the Outeniqua and Tsitsikamma Forests, the then southernmost population left in Africa after their extinction in the Western Cape – the last elephant in the Cape Peninsula was shot in 1704, and the herds in the Overberg area west of Knysna were killed off by 1800. By 1870, only an estimated 400 elephants remained in the area from Knysna to Addo. In 1919, professional hunter Major Philip Jacobus Pretorius was hired by the Cape government to exterminate the last of the elephants. The Administrator of the Cape, Sir Frederic de Waal (De Waal Drive) wanted them completely exterminated. But it was finally decided to leave a small herd of 16 in the Addo Reserve. In just over a year, Pretorius shot 115 elephants. Ever since then, sightings have been elusive, with there generally being believed to be between four and 14 elephants surviving at any one time. A 1970 survey estimated 14 elephants; a 1996 study found that the elephants were functionally extinct, with just one adult female left. In 1986, Daleen Matthee’s book “Circles In A Forest” (Kringe in die Bos) was published, became a best-seller, and was made into a Hollywood movie, and gave new impetus to the plight and conservation of the Knysna elephants. In September 2000, forest guard Wilfred Oraai videotaped a young bull from a distance of about 30 metres. Patterson has collected numerous fresh samples of elephant dung for DNA analysis by geneticist Lori Eggert from the University of Missouri in Columbia, and on this he bases his estimate of at least five females, and at one stage, three bulls and two calves. Despite the DNA evidence, officials insisted only one elephant survived, an elusive female known as 'The Matriarch' or 'Oupoot', making the Knysna elephant functionally extinct. In 1994, three cows were brought from the Kruger National Park and released into a boma at Diepwalle, and then released into the forest. One cow soon died, they were brought to Knysna in the winter. THe other two were very young about 3 years old and they could not keep up with the matriarch who roams about 30 kms everyday. Eventually the remaining two preferred raiding farm pastures to the forests, and they were removed to Shamwari private reserve five years later. Since then, there have been competing claims, the latest being those of Patterson and SANParks this past week: in 2002, sightings suggested there were three elephants; in 2007, faecal DNA analysis pointed at five remaining females, but this was not confirmed by sightings and other evidence; in 2015, 18 months of grid camera trapping of the forests by the Landmark Foundation (Dr Bool Smuts) indicated only one matriarch remained. Pattersons claims have been disputed by scientists saying DNA sampling of elephant dung is far more complex but everyone agrees that SOMETHING has to be done urgently. Since 1994 conservationists have learnt a lot more about elephant relocation and elephants from Addo would be better suited than from Kruger.
